records.place: Haute Vallée du Gassac, Aniane, Hérault, Languedoc

wine.name: Mas de Daumas Gassac Rouge
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, three quarters or more, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Pinot Noir, Tannat and a scatter of rare varieties.
wine.sites: Parcels cut from the garrigue in the narrow, cool valley of the Gassac north of Aniane, on red, powder fine soil of glacial origin.
wine.making: Picked by hand, then given a long, gentle fermentation and maceration in the manner of the Médoc, with soft pumping over. The wine is aged for twelve to fifteen months in oak barrels of one to seven years old and bottled without filtering.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackcurrant leaf and bay over cedar, cold stone and a breath of garrigue thyme; firm, fine grained tannin and fresh acidity give it the shape of a Médoc rather than the warmth of the south.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first years, it opens after about seven and, by the estate's own reckoning, goes on gaining for twenty years and more in a good cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate, named for the Daumas family's old farm and the valley of the Gassac above Aniane.
The IGP and its local name on recent labels; vintages of the early 2000s read Vin de Pays de l'Hérault.
The plain category under which the first vintage, 1978, was bottled in 1980.

records.table: Mas de Daumas Gassac Rouge is the Aniane red, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon from a cool valley of glacial soil, that showed from its first vintage in 1978 that the Languedoc could make wine to age. Sold as IGP, it wants decanting when young.
records.story: At the start of the 1970s Aimé Guibert (1924 to 2016), born in Millau, and his wife bought the Daumas family's farm in the valley of the Gassac above Aniane. A friend, the Bordeaux geographer Henri Enjalbert (1910 to 1983), studied its red, powder fine soil of glacial origin and urged them to plant vines. They planted Cabernet Sauvignon, by the estate's account from cuttings of Bordeaux estates, and made their first vintage in 1978 with advice from the oenologist Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004). It was bottled in 1980 as plain Vin de Table, mostly Cabernet with Malbec, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir and Tannat, since no appellation of the Languedoc allowed such a blend. As the estate tells it, Gault Millau called the 1982 the Lafite of the Languedoc, and a white followed with the 1986 vintage. In May 2001 the Californian house Mondavi gave up a plan to clear and plant the wooded Arboussas massif, common land of Aniane, after two years of dispute in which Guibert led the opposition and a new town council turned against the project. He died in 2016 and his sons carried the estate on. For a sommelier the wine is the founding case for fine Languedoc made outside the appellations.

others.name: Mas de Daumas Gassac Blanc
others.note: The white, first made with the 1986 vintage, a blend of Viognier, Chardonnay, Petit Manseng and many other varieties.

others.name: Cuvée Émile Peynaud

others.name: Moulin de Gassac
others.note: A separate range of the family's, begun in 1991 and sold under its own name.

traps: Daumas Gassac is an IGP wine, never AOP Languedoc: recent labels read Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, those of the early 2000s Vin de Pays de l'Hérault, and the first Vin de Table.
It is led by Cabernet Sauvignon; Grange des Pères, its Aniane neighbour, is built on Syrah and Mourvèdre.
Moulin de Gassac is a separate range, not the Rouge and not a second wine of the estate.

report: The founding year is left empty: the estate's history page and Decanter give 1970, interviews the estate hosts give 1971 (the library's year), and a Midi Libre piece it hosts gives 1972 for the handover; the story says the start of the 1970s.
Guibert's birth in Millau in 1924 rests on The Drinks Business, and his death in May 2016 aged 91 on Decanter and a second notice; his wife and sons are living and are not named.
Enjalbert's dates are Wikipedia's and a 2018 biobibliography on HAL, Université de la Réunion; Peynaud's are Wikipedia's and those the Codex's other flagship records carry.

The grapes, the long maceration, twelve to fifteen months in barrels of one to seven years and the labels by period (Vin de Table 1978, Vin de Pays de l'Hérault in the early 2000s, IGP Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, Cité d'Aniane since) are the estate's vintage pages, read through search; the barrel time is also the importer Polaner's.

The Gault Millau line on the 1982 and the Bordeaux cuttings rest on the estate's own account and are told as such; the Mondavi withdrawal of May 2001, the Arboussas massif as common land and the new town council rest on Decanter, an Inderscience case study and a Gastronomica article.
The library's trap names the IGP Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, and data-advanced.js teaches it as Vin de Pays de l'Hérault or Saint-Guilhem: both are right for different periods, as the record says.
WebFetch of the estate's technical sheet was refused (host not allowed); the serving advice follows the Codex's service reference for a full red, since no estate page found gives one.

wine.name: Grange des Pères Rouge
wine.grapes: Syrah and Mourvèdre, about three quarters between them, with Cabernet Sauvignon and a little Counoise; the shares move from year to year.
wine.sites: Stony limestone hills near Aniane, cleared by the founder and planted from the late 1980s, on clay and limestone with rolled pebbles, a short way from Daumas Gassac.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented parcel by parcel, each variety on its own, with its own yeasts and a long maceration. The wines are raised at length in oak barrels, then blended and rested in vat for some months before bottling, neither fined nor filtered.
wine.glass: Black plum, blackberry and black olive over liquorice, garrigue and a smoky, meaty note of Mourvèdre; dense and savoury, with ripe, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and closed when released after its long élevage, it gains savoury depth over ten years and more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.term: Domaine de la Grange des Pères
label.means: The estate at Aniane in the Hérault, whose first vintage was 1992.
The geographical indication of the Hérault department, used because the blend falls outside AOP Languedoc.
The older name of the same category, on the labels of earlier vintages.

records.table: Grange des Pères is the Aniane estate whose red, Syrah and Mourvèdre with Cabernet Sauvignon and a little Counoise, is raised at length in barrel and sold as IGP Pays d'Hérault. Dense, dark and savoury, it wants decanting and time in the cellar.
records.story: Before he planted a vine of his own, the founder of Grange des Pères worked in three cellars of note: with the Chave family in Hermitage, at Coche-Dury in Meursault and at Domaine de Trévallon in Provence. He then cleared stony limestone hills near Aniane and planted them from the late 1980s, taking his Syrah cuttings from Hermitage and his Cabernet Sauvignon from Trévallon, as most accounts tell it. The first vintage came in 1992, a red of Mourvèdre, Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon; Counoise appears in the later blends. Because Cabernet Sauvignon has no place in the Languedoc appellation, the wine was sold as a Vin de Pays de l'Hérault, the category since renamed IGP, as Mas de Daumas Gassac, a short way off, had been sold outside the appellations since 1978. The making held to one pattern: each variety picked and fermented apart, a long time in barrel, then a rest in vat, with no fining or filtering. A white of Roussanne, Marsanne and Chardonnay was made beside the red. The founder died in 2021, and his brother carried the domaine on. For a sommelier Grange des Pères and Daumas Gassac stand together as the Aniane pair: two estates that made their names in the Languedoc with no appellation behind them.

others.name: Grange des Pères Blanc
others.note: The white, led by Roussanne with Marsanne and Chardonnay, raised in barrel like the red.

traps: Grange des Pères is IGP Pays d'Hérault, not an AOP: the Cabernet Sauvignon in the blend keeps it outside AOP Languedoc.
Domaine de la Grange des Pères in Aniane has nothing to do with Penfolds Grange, the Shiraz of South Australia.
Syrah and Mourvèdre lead here; Mas de Daumas Gassac, a short way off, is led by Cabernet Sauvignon.

report: The plan's note says the founder is living: he died on 30 April 2021 (Decanter, iDealwine, wein.plus); his birth year is 1962 or 1963 by the reported ages, so he is described rather than named, and his brother, who is living, is not named.

The founding year is left empty: the library gives 1992 and plants from 1992, but the sources give the first vines in 1988 after three years of clearing (one account) or a founding in 1989, with 1992 the first vintage in every account; the record says planted from the late 1980s and first vintage 1992.

The library's trap calls the red Mourvèdre led; the shares found run from Syrah and Mourvèdre equal to Syrah ahead or Mourvèdre ahead by vintage, so the record says Syrah and Mourvèdre about three quarters between them.

The founder's work with the Chave family, at Coche-Dury and at Trévallon, and the cuttings from Hermitage and Trévallon rest on several retailers' and importers' accounts and Decanter's profile; a claim of Chardonnay cuttings from Coche-Dury rests on one and is left out.

The estate has no website found, so no primary source stands; the making (separate vinification, own yeasts, long barrel ageing then vat, unfined and unfiltered) rests on two retailers' accounts, and a figure of 24 months in 228 litre barrels on one only, so it is left out.
Decanter's profile dates a family property bought by the founder's grandfather in 1958; one source only, left out.

wine.name: Mas Jullien Autour de Jonquières
wine.grapes: Mourvèdre, Carignan and Syrah; blends made before 2017 also held Grenache and Cinsault.
wine.sites: About a dozen lieux-dits around Jonquières and its neighbouring villages, as the name says, on the varied hill soils below the Larzac plateau.
wine.making: Extraction is gentle, with punching down of the cap and pumping over, and the wine then spends about two years in large oak casks before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Black cherry, bramble and dried thyme over liquorice, warm stone and a salty, savoury edge; medium to full in body, with fresh acidity and fine, firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Open enough after a few years in bottle, it gains savoury depth over a decade and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large red wine glass.

label.means: A red wine appellation of the hills below the Larzac plateau, its own AOP by a decree of October 2014.
Around Jonquières: a blend of parcels around the village and its neighbours rather than a single site.
The older appellation on earlier labels, of which Terrasses du Larzac was a named part from 2004.

records.table: Mas Jullien's Autour de Jonquières is a red of the Terrasses du Larzac, Mourvèdre, Carignan and Syrah from parcels around the village of Jonquières, raised about two years in large oak. Expect dark fruit, dried herbs and a fresh, savoury finish.
records.story: Jonquières lies in the hills below the Larzac plateau in the Hérault, country whose growers long sent their grapes to the co-operative. In 1985 the founder, the son of a grower family, chose not to follow that road and set up his own estate in the village, bottling wine from its hill parcels under the Coteaux du Languedoc appellation. His father later made and bottled his own wine too, at Mas Cal Demoura in the same village. The house came to be counted among the pioneers of the Languedoc's revival, beside Mas de Daumas Gassac. The hills around it gained a name of their own: in 2004 Terrasses du Larzac first appeared on labels as a named part of the Coteaux du Languedoc, and a decree of 17 October 2014 made it an appellation in its own right, for red wine only. Autour de Jonquières, the house's principal red, takes its name from its making: a blend of about a dozen lieux-dits around the village and its neighbours. Before 2017 the blend also held Grenache and Cinsault; since then the founder has given more room to Mourvèdre beside Carignan and Syrah. For a sommelier it shows the Terrasses du Larzac as the hills make it: fresh, savoury and built to keep.

Autour de Jonquières is a blend of parcels around the village, not a single vineyard.
Mas Cal Demoura, also in Jonquières, began as the founder's father's estate and is a separate house from Mas Jullien.

report: The library gives Autour de Jonquières as Carignan, Cinsault, Syrah and Mourvèdre; a merchant's sheet gives Carignan, Mourvèdre and Syrah, and Vinous says Grenache and Cinsault left the blend before 2017 in favour of Mourvèdre, so the record gives the recent blend and names the earlier grapes.

The barrel time rests on Vinous (two years in large casks) and iDealwine's sheet for the 2021 (a year in demi-muids, then a year in foudres after blending); iDealwine's page is not cited because its address names the living founder, and one merchant gives 12 to 18 months in French oak, so the record says about two years in large oak.
The 2014 decree (no. 2014-1200 of 17 October 2014) is the INAO specification's; the 2004 first use on labels is the appellation body's and INAO's presentation; red wine only is the specification's.

The founder's break from the co-operative in 1985 rests on a producer profile and Wikipedia's Mas Cal Demoura page, and the father's estate at Mas Cal Demoura on Wikipedia and an importer's page; the founder's age in 1985 and the soils by parcel (one source) are left out.

The library's why says the founder's argument is the reasoning behind the appellation itself; no source found says so, so the story says only that the house was counted among the pioneers of the revival (Wikipedia's Terrasses du Larzac page).
Lous Rougeos and Carlan are named as cuvées of the house by an Italian merchant; what sets each apart was not sourced and is not said.
No page of the estate itself was found; the founder is living and is never named.

wine.name: Muntada
wine.grapes: Grenache Noir and very old Carignan, in about equal parts, with a little Mourvèdre and Syrah.
wine.sites: Old vines on the hills around Calce, about twenty kilometres north west of Perpignan, on limestone, schist and clay; some of the house's vines are more than a century old, by its own account.
wine.making: Made in the house's way, with much use of whole bunches and little sulphur, it is raised for about thirty months in foudres and barrels and bottled without fining or filtering.
wine.glass: Deep ruby; black cherry and violet over dried thyme, liquorice and a stony, saline note; supple and fresh rather than heavy, with fine, chalky tannin and a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable after decanting in its youth, it gains savoury depth over ten years and more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so; a large red wine glass.

label.means: A red only appellation of the Pyrénées-Orientales, recognised by a decree of 28 March 1977.
The IGP of the Roussillon, on several of the house's labels, Les Calcinaires among them.
The family estate at Calce in the Agly valley, whose name the label carries.

records.table: Muntada is Domaine Gauby's red from old vines on the hills above Calce, Grenache and very old Carignan with touches of Mourvèdre and Syrah, raised thirty months in foudres and barrels. It shows dry Roussillon fresh and supple rather than heavy.
records.story: Calce is a small village of the Agly valley, in the hills north west of Perpignan, where the Roussillon's dry reds long stood in the shadow of its vins doux naturels. A decree of 28 March 1977 created the Côtes du Roussillon Villages appellation, for red wine only, and gave the hill villages a name for their dry reds. In 1985, as most accounts date it, the founder took over his family's small holding of vines at Calce and began to make and bottle wine of his own. He farmed by organic principles and later by biodynamic ones, and the house came to leave much of its land wild, garrigue and woods with other crops among the vines. Over the years the house turned from power towards freshness, with whole bunches, little sulphur and less alcohol, and the estate was counted among the pioneers of dry Roussillon. Muntada, drawn from Grenache and Carignan of great age, became its flagship red, sold as Côtes du Roussillon Villages and raised for about thirty months in foudres and barrels. For a sommelier Muntada answers the guest who knows the Roussillon only for Banyuls and Maury: a dry red of the hills, fresh, supple and long.

wine.name: Maury 10 Ans d'Âge, Cuvée Spéciale
wine.grapes: Grenache Noir, by far the greater part, from the estate's old bush vines.
wine.sites: Old Grenache trained as bush vines, many of them over forty years old, on the black schist around the village of Maury.
wine.making: The fermenting must is muted with neutral grape spirit, which stops the yeasts and keeps the grape's own sugar. In the house's oxidative way the wine then spends a year outdoors in glass bonbonnes, through summer sun and winter cold, and years in large old oak foudres before it is blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Brick and tawny; prune, dried fig and roasted coffee over cocoa, walnut and orange peel, sweet but kept lively by the spirit, with a long, nutty finish of rancio.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink when bottled after its years in cask, it keeps for years in bottle and changes slowly once open.
wine.serve: About 15 degrees Celsius, as the house advises for its aged Maury, the bottle opened an hour ahead; no need to decant; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The appellation of the Maury vineyards in the Roussillon, for vin doux naturel; its dry red is Maury Sec.
A wine muted with grape spirit during fermentation, so that it keeps the grape's own sugar.
An age statement of ten years; the house also bottles Maury of twenty, thirty and forty years.

records.table: Mas Amiel's Maury 10 Ans d'Âge is Grenache muted with spirit, left a year outdoors in glass bonbonnes and then aged in large old oak foudres. Serve it cool, at about 15 degrees, with blue cheese or a chocolate pudding.
records.story: As the house tells it, the estate began with a game of cards. In 1816 a Bishop of Perpignan staked the Domaine des Goudous at the table and lost it to an engineer of the state's roads and bridges service, whose surname, Amiel, the estate has carried since; nobody knows quite what passed at the table. Its wine rested on a far older idea, mutage, the stopping of fermentation with spirit, which the house traces to a Montpellier physician of 1285. Early in the twentieth century a banker bought the estate, and his family held it through the century until the last of the line died in 1997. The house made its name with Maury aged in the open air: Grenache muted with spirit, set out for a year in glass bonbonnes in sun and frost, then kept for years in the large old oak foudres of its cellar. In 1999 the estate was sold to a buyer from outside the family. Its range sets the oxidative wines beside a young, fruit led Vintage and dry reds. For a sommelier the ten year old shows the oxidative style of Maury plainly: Grenache turned towards prune, coffee and walnut by air and time.

others.name: Maury Vintage
others.note: The young, fruit led style: Grenache muted and bottled early, without the years of open air ageing.

others.name: Maury 20, 30 and 40 Ans d'Âge
others.note: Older blends of the same oxidative making, a year in bonbonnes and then decades in oak foudres.

others.name: Vintage Charles Dupuy
others.note: A Vintage Maury named for the banker who bought the estate, muted midway through fermentation and raised in new barrels.

traps: Maury Sec is the appellation's dry red, separate from the fortified Maury and not a vin doux naturel.
Rancio, the nutty taste of long oxidative ageing, is sought in aged Maury, not a fault.
Maury lies inland, on schist in the hills of the Roussillon; Banyuls, also a Grenache vin doux naturel, lies on the coast.

cards.front: Mas Amiel: where does its aged Maury spend its first year after muting?
cards.back: Outdoors, in glass bonbonnes, through summer sun and winter cold, before years in large oak foudres.

cards.front: Mas Amiel: at what temperature does the house advise serving its aged Maury?
cards.back: About 15 degrees Celsius, the bottle opened an hour ahead.

questions.q: A guest asks what gives Mas Amiel's Maury 10 Ans d'Âge its notes of prune, coffee and walnut. Which answer fits?
opts: A year in glass bonbonnes outdoors, then years in old foudres
Grapes dried on straw mats before pressing
Ageing under a veil of flor yeast in a solera
A long maceration of Muscat skins before muting
questions.exp: The muted Grenache is aged oxidatively, a year in bonbonnes in sun and cold and then years in large oak; a flor wine ages under yeast in a solera, which is the way of Jerez.

questions.q: As Mas Amiel tells it, how did the estate pass in 1816 to the engineer whose name it carries?
opts: He won it from a bishop in a game of cards
He bought it from a family of bankers
He received it as payment for building a bridge
He inherited it from an uncle in Perpignan
questions.exp: The house tells of a bishop who lost the Domaine des Goudous at cards in 1816; a banker bought the estate only early in the twentieth century.

report: Pick in doubt: the estate's own shop lists its aged Maury as 20, 30 and 40 Ans d'Âge and single vintages, and no 10 Ans d'Âge; the Cuvée Spéciale 10 Ans d'Âge appears in Hachette's 2019 guide and wine databases, so it may be discontinued. Proposed swap: the house's Maury 20 Ans d'Âge, whose making, blend and serving the estate's own page gives, for the checker of the chunk.

The grapes of the 10 Ans d'Âge are given as Grenache in the databases; the estate gives its 20 and 30 Ans d'Âge as about nine parts Grenache Noir with Macabeu and Carignan, so the record says Grenache Noir, by far the greater part.

The year in bonbonnes and then 350 hl foudres is the estate's for its 20 and 30 Ans d'Âge and a merchant's account of the house's aged range; the record tells it as the house's oxidative way, not as a figure for the ten year old.
The serving at 15 degrees, opened an hour ahead, and the pairings with blue cheese and chocolate are the estate's for its 20 Ans d'Âge.

The banker of the early twentieth century is Charles Dupuy by the estate's history, but his birth year was not found, so he is described; the estate says he died in 1916, while Gault&Millau and iDealwine say the last of the Dupuy line died in 1997 and the estate was sold in 1999; the dates of the purchase differ (1907 or about 1911), so the story says early in the twentieth century. The buyer of 1999 is living and is not named.
Maury's recognition in 1936 and Maury Sec's in 2011 rest on secondary sources only (Hachette, Wine with Seth, a glossary) and were left out; the phylloxera date of 1865 (one source) is left out.
Searches for this record: 10 of the group's 31; the house's Maury pages were read through search and the 10 Ans d'Âge has no page of its own on the estate's site.
